an3.72:1.1: I have heard that on one occasion Ven. Ānanda was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.
an3.72:1.2: Then a certain householder, a disciple of the Fatalists [Ājīvakas], went to him and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there he said to Ven. Ānanda,
an3.72:2.1: “Among us, sir, whose Dhamma is well-taught?
an3.72:2.2: Who has practiced well in this world?
an3.72:2.3: Who in the world is Well-Gone?”
an3.72:2.4: “In that case, householder, I will question you in return. Answer as you see fit.
an3.72:2.6: Those who teach a Dhamma for the abandoning of passion, for the abandoning of aversion, for the abandoning of delusion—is their Dhamma well-taught or not?
an3.72:2.7: Or how does this strike you?”
an3.72:2.8: “Sir, those who teach a Dhamma for the abandoning of passion, for the abandoning of aversion, for the abandoning of delusion—their Dhamma is well-taught.
an3.72:3.2: Those who have practiced for the abandoning of passion, for the abandoning of aversion, for the abandoning of delusion—have they practiced well in this world or not?
an3.72:3.3: Or how does this strike you?”
an3.72:3.4: “Sir, those who have practiced for the abandoning of passion, for the abandoning of aversion, for the abandoning of delusion—they have practiced well in this world.
an3.72:4.2: Those whose passion is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising; those whose aversion is abandoned… whose delusion is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising—are they, in this world, Well-Gone or not?
an3.72:4.3: Or how does this strike you?”
an3.72:4.4: “Sir, those whose passion… aversion… delusion is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising—they, in this world, are Well-Gone.
an3.72:5.1: “In this way, householder, you have answered yourself:
an3.72:5.2: ‘Those who teach a Dhamma for the abandoning of passion, for the abandoning of aversion, for the abandoning of delusion—their Dhamma is well-taught.
an3.72:5.4: Those who have practiced for the abandoning of passion, for the abandoning of aversion, for the abandoning of delusion—they have practiced well in this world.
an3.72:5.6: Those whose passion… aversion… delusion is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising—they, in this world, are Well-Gone.’”
an3.72:6.2: that there is neither extolling of one’s own Dhamma nor deprecation of another’s,
an3.72:6.3: but just the teaching of the Dhamma in its proper sphere, speaking to the point without mentioning oneself.
an3.72:6.4: “You, venerable sir, teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of passion… aversion… delusion.
an3.72:6.6: You have practiced for the abandoning of passion… aversion… delusion.
an3.72:6.7: You have practiced well in this world.
an3.72:6.8: Your passion… aversion… delusion is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.
an3.72:6.9: You, in this world, are Well-Gone.
an3.72:7.2: Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Ānanda—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.
an3.72:7.3: I go to the Buddha for refuge, to the Dhamma, & to the Saṅgha of monks.
an3.72:7.4: May Master Ānanda remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for life.”
